structural_memory.memory: Shipboard digital risk has distinct owner/manager, master/crew, technical IT/OT support, equipment OEM or vendor support, system-integrator, shore IT/security and assurance roles. Responsibility for operations, access, configuration and incident support can cross organizational boundaries without being equivalent to system ownership.

Asset inventory is a lifecycle state, not a static device list. Installed hardware, software/firmware, logical services, ownership/support responsibility and criticality can diverge from documentation after replacements, temporary equipment or upgrades.

IT/OT network or zone/interface architecture is a boundary-management state rather than a topology fact to publish. The useful structural memory is whether intended trust/interface boundaries and interdependencies are known, current and controlled; exact addresses, routes and diagrams are deferred.

Identity and access have join/change/revoke and privilege states. Account existence, authorization, authentication mechanism and actual session/use should remain separately clocked, especially across crew turnover, shore support and vendor access.

Vendor remote connectivity is an operational-support dependency with enabled/disabled, authorized-window, session/approval and support-availability states. Remote capability can improve repairability while also requiring explicit governance; no technical connection details are retained.

Configuration and software/firmware version baselines are separate from physical hardware condition. Intended/approved version, installed version, pending change and verified post-change behavior can diverge in time.

Patch or update governance is a controlled-change lifecycle rather than a simple latest/not-latest flag. Availability, applicability assessment, compatibility/testing, approval, deployment, fallback and verification can occur on different clocks, especially for operational technology.

Backup state and recovery capability are different. A backup can exist while being stale, incomplete or unverified for restoration; recovery readiness requires scope, known-good reference, accessibility and tested restore confidence without exposing implementation details.

Logging/monitoring is an observation layer with coverage and known-time. The existence of logs or alarms is not proof that an event was detected, understood or attributable; monitoring gaps and later reconstruction must remain explicit.

A cyber or digital anomaly lifecycle can be represented defensively as observation/triage, scope assessment, containment decision, continuity workaround, recovery/restoration and post-event review. This pass retains no attack method, exploit path or tactical response procedure.

Business/operational continuity during digital degradation is a separate state from cyber cause attribution. Navigation, cargo, machinery support, communications or administration may be degraded to different degrees while root cause remains uncertain.

Controlled change and configuration-management records matter to historical replay: planned change, emergency change, implementation, validation and rollback/recovery should be temporally distinct so later stability does not rewrite what was known at the change point.

Third-party and lifecycle obsolescence risk crosses cyber and equipment support: unsupported operating environments, discontinued vendor support or incompatible dependencies can increase recovery friction even without a known incident or hardware defect.

P067 software/firmware supportability should distinguish vendor-support state from shipboard authorization and installed-configuration state; a vendor can offer an update or remote service without the vessel having assessed, approved or deployed it.

P026/P027-style digital observations and alarms should not be treated as independent corroboration merely because they appear in multiple systems; shared networks, clocks, software or upstream sensors can create common-mode information dependencies.

Technical availability should separate digital-control degradation from underlying machinery condition. A mechanically sound function may become unavailable through control/configuration/support loss, while a cyber alert does not by itself prove physical malfunction.

Incident recovery should preserve both service restoration time and confidence/verification state; restored output is not automatically proof that configuration integrity, data completeness or root cause has been fully established.
Software/firmware version and vendor-support states partially overlap the marine-equipment lifecycle recovered in P067.
Alarm/log observation versus interpretation and shared digital dependencies overlap earlier instrumentation, alarm and evidence-integrity memory.

reviewed_no_specific_memory: Exact network diagrams, addresses, credentials, access-control settings and remote-access implementation are intentionally not retained.
Exact software/firmware versions, patch levels, vulnerabilities, exploits, malware, indicators and incident tactics require authoritative security-safe Evidence and are outside this blind pass.
Named ship systems, cyber vendors, managed-service providers, integrators and forensic firms are not retained as a provider or target directory.
Named incidents, affected vessels, causal attribution, loss amounts, regulatory findings and current cyber posture require claim-scoped Evidence.
negative_space: Exact technical topology, credentials, vulnerabilities, exploitability and security-control configurations.
Named shipboard IT/OT products and current software/patch/support status.
Private/regional maritime cyber, remote-support, managed-service and forensic provider lineages.
Historical non-English predecessor terminology for shipboard automation networking, remote support and cyber incidents.
epistemic_boundary: Memory-only defensive orientation/source-discovery output. It is not cybersecurity, incident-response, network, engineering, navigation or operational advice and does not expose or establish any topology, credential, vulnerability, exploit, named system, provider, incident, attribution or current security-posture fact.
stop_reason: The defensive shipboard IT/OT governance lifecycle is recalled at useful structural resolution. Further detail would become topology-, credential-, vulnerability-, exploit-, product-, incident-, provider- or jurisdiction-specific and is intentionally deferred rather than converted into operational cyber guidance.
